doc.title: Jon Hendricks interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 29, 2000 [interview 2 of 2]

title: Scatting with Charlie Parker in Toledo
summary: Sat in with Bird's group, who told him he was a jazz singer and to come to New York.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy

blocks.x: Kenny Dorham had just replaced Miles. So Bird had finished playing and he told me, so that I scatted. I scatted about ten choruses. I didn’t know when to stop. I was looking for a place to stop.

So finally I said that’s enough, you’d better stop, so I quit. And Kenny Dorham got up from his chair next to Bird and he was starting to play his solo, and I started to leave the bandstand. And I felt this tug on my coattail. I’m trying to leave, and this — and I look and there’s Bird and he’s got ahold of my coattail, and so I turned back. You know I’ve been in show business all my life so I made it look like I’d just changed my mind, because of the audience. So I turned back and he says to sit in the chair next to him. So I sit there, you know Max is playing, Curly Russell is plucking, the piano player was Al Haig, he’s chording, and the music is going on, and Kenny is soloing. And so Bird is looking out at the audience, and I’m over here and he says, “hey man, what do you do?” I said, “I’m a law student.” And he looks at me. “A law student?” I said, “yeah.” He says, “man, you ain’t no lawyer.” I said, “oh yeah, what am I?” He says, “you’re a jazz singer.” I said, “so what do I do about that?” I’m condescending to him, I’m humoring to him. And he says, “well, you’ve got to come to New York.” So I thought New York, 13 million people. A million people a day pass through there. I said, “I don’t know anybody in New York.” He says, “well you know me.” I said, “well where will I find you?” He says, “just ask anybody.” So I figured to myself, I says this guy’s nuts. And so then I get up to leave and I says, “thanks.” He says, “not at all.” He says, “you know when you get to New York look me up.” I say, “okay.” And I was trying to get out of there. So I got off the bandstand, my knees were shaking, and I was thinking what kind of cat is that? Just ask anybody. Whoa. So I forgot it. Because I was into my studies and I was into local politics at that time and I was attracting a lot of attention from the local politicians because I was getting a 3.5 average, I had the highest grades in the pre-law college. So they were all tapping me for going into politics and all that. So I was busy with a lot of stuff and I was trying to make a living and I had a son by that time, a young boy, he was three years old. So I’m trying to support my family and I didn’t think about anything like what he said. So two years and four months went by. And I got involved in the local legal scene around there and found that it was very racist. And they were not going to put me in the position that I had earned. By getting the 3.5 average, the highest grades, you immediately inherit the job of juvenile state probation officer, that’s the way it’s been awarded for 20 years previously. The highest graded pre-law student got that job. So when they awarded it to me, it meant that I would be on a social equal with all the juvenile court judges and their wives. And my wife was Irish.
